EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  
Oregon Health Insurance Experiment (Medicaid Lottery)

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Use the lottery as a source of randomly assigned exogenous variation:

• Intent-to-Treat (ITT): difference in outcomes between lottery winners and losers.  
• Treatment-on-the-Treated (TOT, or Local Average Treatment Effect): two-stage least squares (2SLS) that instruments Medicaid coverage with lottery assignment.  

Because assignment is random, ITT is unbiased. 2SLS corrects for incomplete take-up and delivers the causal effect of Medicaid for compliers (those who enroll if and only if they win).

Why appropriate?  
– Randomization eliminates selection on observables and unobservables.  
– Administrative and survey outcomes are observed after assignment, so reverse causality is impossible.  
– Non-compliance is handled cleanly with IV.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable  
• Z = 1 if individual’s reservation-list ID was drawn in the 2008 lottery (offers the chance to apply for Medicaid).  
• D = 1 if individual is actually enrolled in Medicaid at any point during the follow-up window.

Control group  
• Z = 0 individuals whose lottery numbers were not drawn.

Key variation / timing  
• Single lottery wave (May–Sept 2008).  
• Outcomes measured over the 12 months after the lottery date (administrative) and in the mail survey fielded ~1 year post-lottery.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Random Assignment: Z is independent of potential outcomes and baseline covariates.  
 Plausible: state conducted computerized random draws; balance tests should confirm.

A2. Exclusion Restriction: Z affects outcomes only through Medicaid coverage (no direct effect).  
 Plausible but needs discussion (e.g., “winning” might change expectations or information). Administrative outcomes largely immune; still defend with evidence that winners who fail to enroll look like losers.

A3. First Stage / Relevance: P(D = 1 | Z = 1) – P(D = 1 | Z = 0) ≈ 0.25, F-stat≫10.  
 Documented by state records.

A4. Monotonicity: No one loses Medicaid because they win the lottery (no “defiers”).  
 Highly plausible.

A5. SUTVA: One applicant’s lottery outcome does not alter another’s potential outcomes except through that person’s own insurance status.  
 Potential household spillovers minimal; address by household-level clustering.

A6. Balanced Attrition: Survey response not differentially driven by outcomes conditional on Z.  
 Check response rates by Z and re-weight using administrative variables.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Main Threats & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Survey Non-response (26 % response)  
 • Compare baseline/admin variables of responders across Z (test differential attrition).  
 • Re-weight survey using inverse-probability weights based on response propensity.  
 • Replicate core results in administrative data with ≈ 100 % coverage.

T2. Control-group Insurance Take-up / Cross-overs  
 • Handled by IV; effects still causal for compliers.  
 • Report ITT and TOT; show robustness to redefining D as “any public insurance” or “any insurance”.

T3. Exclusion Violation via Information or Anticipation Effects  
 • Test whether lottery win changes outcomes immediately (before enrollment can occur).  
 • Include controls for any other contemporaneous programs.  
 • Bounding analysis: restrict to winners who actually submitted an application but were denied (placebo).

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# 0. Packages -------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)     # fast IV + clustering
library(modelsummary)

# 1. Load Data ------------------------------------------------------------
admin   <- read_csv("oregon_admin_12m.csv")    # enrollment + claims + credit
survey  <- read_csv("oregon_survey.csv")       # self-reported measures
baseline<- read_csv("oregon_baseline.csv")     # demographics at signup

# 2. Merge & Keep Analysis Sample ----------------------------------------
data <- baseline %>%
  left_join(admin , by = "person_id") %>%
  left_join(survey, by = "person_id") %>%
  mutate(
    Z  = as.integer(lottery_win == 1),
    D  = as.integer(medicaid_enrolled == 1),          # first-stage variable
    any_er = as.integer(er_visits > 0),
    med_debt_coll = as.integer(med_debt_collections > 0)
  )

# 3. First-Stage ----------------------------------------------------------
fs <- feols(D ~ Z | household_id, data = data)
etable(fs)

# 4. Main IV Specification -----------------------------------------------
# Example outcome: any ER visit
iv1 <- feols(any_er ~ 1 | Z | D ~ Z,        # y ~ 1, IV syntax: y | X | endog ~ IV
             cluster = ~household_id, data = data)
etable(iv1, fitstat = c("ivf", "n","r2"))

# 5. ITT for comparison ---------------------------------------------------
itt1 <- feols(any_er ~ Z, cluster = ~household_id, data = data)

# 6. Add baseline covariates (robustness) ---------------------------------
baseline_vars <- c("age","female","white","prior_er_use")
formula_cov   <- as.formula(
  paste0("any_er ~ ", paste0(baseline_vars, collapse = "+"), " | Z | D ~ Z")
)
iv2 <- feols(formula_cov, cluster = ~household_id, data = data)

# 7. Attrition Weighting Robustness ---------------------------------------
# create response weight for survey vars
resp_model <- glm(response_ind ~ Z + age + female + county, 
                  family = binomial, data = data)
data$w <- 1 / fitted(resp_model)

iv_weighted <- feols(self_rated_health ~ 1 | Z | D ~ Z, 
                     weights = ~w, cluster = ~household_id, data = data)

# 8. Summarise ------------------------------------------------------------
modelsummary(list(ITT = itt1, IV = iv1, IV_cov = iv2),
             stars = TRUE, gof_omit = "Adj|AIC|BIC")
```
Notes:  
• `feols` syntax allows IV with `y ~ controls | IVs | endog ~ instrument`.  
• Clustering at household removes intra-household correlation.  
• `etable` prints first-stage F.  
• Repeat loop over outcomes (outpatient, Rx fills, debt, etc.).  

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results (Prior)
────────────────────────────────────────
Direction: Medicaid increases health-care utilization, lowers financial strain, and modestly improves self-reported physical/mental health.  

Approximate magnitudes (one-year horizon, TOT):  
• +35 % outpatient visits (≈ 1.2 additional visits).  
• +15 % probability of any ER visit (≈ 4 pp).  
• –25 % probability of medical debt in collections (≈ 6 pp).  
• +0.10 SD improvement in self-reported health or depression score.  

Economic intuition: Lower out-of-pocket price → higher demand for care; insurance dampens financial risk; health improvements limited in short run but detectible for mental health.

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable/absent)

1. Random assignment verified by balance tests ............. 1  
2. Strong first stage (F > 10) ............................. 1  
3. Exclusion restriction plausibility ...................... 0.8  
4. No differential attrition / survey bias ................. 0.6  
5. SUTVA & no spillovers ................................... 0.9  

Average score ............................................... 0.86  

Overall, the randomized lottery with IV adjustment provides a highly credible design; remaining concerns center on survey attrition and possible small exclusion-restriction violations, both of which can be probed through the robustness checks outlined above.
